growth_story.headline: After shrinking through most of the 1990s, North Macedonia has grown steadily since 1999, though more slowly of late as emigration thins the workforce.
growth_story.arc: North Macedonia's income per person shrank by 1.8 percent a year from 1991 to 1998, as the shock of transition, a closed Greek border and the UN embargo on Serbia hurt trade, and it hit bottom in 1995. From 1999 to 2025 it grew by 3.1 percent a year, a run broken by the 2001 armed conflict (-3.5 in 2001) and the 2020 pandemic (-3.7). Growth was fastest before the global financial crisis and peaked at 7.1 percent in 2007, helped by reforms, foreign investment and closer ties with the EU. Growth has since been steady but slower, averaging 3.7 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 2.7 over 2016–2025. The IMF and World Bank link the slowdown to weak productivity growth after the crisis and to emigration and ageing, which are shrinking the workforce. In 2025 income per person reached its highest level so far, as infrastructure investment and household spending drove growth.

threads.title: Transition slump and blockades
threads.text: After independence, income per person fell every year from 1991 to 1995 and only began to edge up in 1996. The IMF points to political shocks: the closed Greek border, the UN embargo on Serbia and the Kosovo crisis. These hit an economy that rested on a few old sectors such as farming, steel and textiles.

threads.title: Boom, then a slower decade
threads.text: Income per person grew by 5 percent or more a year from 2004 to 2008, a period the IMF says was aided by reforms, foreign investment and EU integration. After the global crisis, growth slowed: income per person barely grew in 2009 and dipped in 2012. The IMF links the slowdown to weaker demand abroad and uncertainty in the region.

threads.title: Weak productivity growth
threads.text: In the decade after the global crisis, the IMF finds that productivity's contribution to growth turned negative and adding capital did more of the work. The World Bank finds productivity growth negative since the 2010s, with only a small gain after the pandemic. The IMF notes that tax breaks for export-focused foreign investors in a few industries created few links with local firms.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 income per person grew by 3.7 percent, the fastest since 2021, as infrastructure investment and household spending lifted demand. The World Bank reports that growth slowed early in 2026 amid geopolitical headwinds, then rebounded in the second quarter, while inflation pressures returned.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes growth that lags behind faster Western Balkan peers. The data tell a kinder story: income per person grew 3.1 percent a year from 1999 to 2025, and over 2016–2025 it grew 2.7 percent a year. That is at the convergence expectation and above the Europe and Central Asia median of 2.0. Part of the gap is about what is measured. The sources mostly look at the size of the whole economy, while emigration shrinks the population, so income per person can rise faster than total output. The sources also compare the country with neighbours that grew faster, not with the wider region.
